title: How to decide if a big long-term investment is worthwhile (without expected value)
summary: Jason Cohen argues expected value misleads for one-shot, all-in investments like a career path or startup, since a guaranteed $1M and a 10% shot at $10M are not equivalent. He offers a framework: outsized payoff, accumulating value, stable conditions over ten years, alignment with global trends, a personal edge, and fit with your long-term vision.

principles.text: Expected value is the wrong tool for big, singular investments; it only works across many uncorrelated bets.
principles.quote: There is one case where expected value is the right tool: A portfolio of bets.

principles.text: Require an outsized payoff, and estimate it to the nearest power of ten, rounding down rather than up.
principles.quote: When it can pay off 10x or 100x, or when it can be life-altering, then even if you fall short of the goal--only 3x or only life-improving--then it was still worthwhile.

principles.text: Pick investments where value accumulates and doesn't erode, ideally with a positive feedback loop. Consulting doesn't compound like SaaS.
principles.quote: At a minimum, value must accrete, but ideally you construct a positive feedback loop, where growth or size itself begets more growth.

principles.text: Invest in what won't change over ten years, since the world must still value it when your payoff arrives.
principles.quote: If you spend 3-5 years investing, expecting a payoff in the subsequent 5 years, the world had better still value that thing during years 5-10.

principles.text: Pick a large, growing market so you answer 'why buy from me' instead of 'why buy at all'.
principles.quote: It means people are already spending money, so you're answering "why buy from me" rather than "why should I allocate budget for this at all"

principles.text: Build an edge by being top 25% at a few uncorrelated things; passion alone doesn't lower risk or raise payoff.
principles.quote: The other way, and the way available to all of us, is to be in the top 25% at a few uncorrelated things, which together creates a special edge.
